senses.definition: (dated) Similar contagious skin diseases causing light patches of scaly skin, particularly psoriasis, syphilis, vitiligo, scabies, and the various diseases considered "tzaraath" in the Old Testament.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Anything considered similarly permanent, harmful, and communicable, particularly when such a thing should be handled by avoidance or isolation of its victims.
senses.example: Sin is a spiritual leprosy.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of murine leprosy or feline leprosy (“diseases caused in rodents and cats by Mycobacterium lepraemurium”).
Synonym of mange and glanders in horses.
Synonym of leprosarium: a place for the housing of lepers in isolation from the rest of society.
An infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae, gradually producing nerve damage and patches of skin necrosis and historically handled by permanently quarantining its sufferers.
A contagious disease causing similar effects in animals, particularly.

core.definition: A chronic infectious disease that damages skin, nerves, and sometimes limbs, caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ro' is a quick reduced vowel, so say 'LEP-ruh-see' and don't pronounce it as 'lep-ROH-see.' The r is American, so it is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a serious disease and carries historical stigma.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'leprosy' in medical, historical, and religious contexts, but in clinical settings they often say 'Hansen's disease' to reduce stigma. The word can appear in news about global health, and it is often used with the term 'Hansen's disease' in US health materials. Figurative uses are rare and usually sound dramatic.

distinctions.note: Hansen's disease is the modern medical name, preferred by many US health agencies, while leprosy is the older, more widely known name.
Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune skin condition and is not infectious, while leprosy is caused by bacteria and affects nerves.

examples.everyday: My aunt was reading about a village where leprosy used to be common, and she was surprised how much has changed.
examples.professional: The health ministry's report tracks new leprosy cases and confirms that early treatment prevents lasting nerve damage.
examples.analytical: The biblical term for skin disease is broader than modern leprosy, so careful exegesis must distinguish the ancient category from the specific bacterial infection.

nuance.analogy: Leprosy is like a slow leak in a pipe: the damage builds quietly until it is visible and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin lepra, from Greek lepra, referring to scaly skin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'lep-ROH-see' with stress on the middle syllable.
Using 'leprosy' as a casual metaphor for any harmful thing, which sounds harsh in US conversation.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'tsara'ath' in the Old Testament covers several skin diseases and affections of cloth and houses, so it is broader than modern leprosy. Leviticus 13:1-46 (RSV) gives detailed priestly rules for diagnosing and isolating people with these conditions. 2 Kings 5:1-14 (RSV) tells how Naaman was healed of his skin disease after obeying Elisha's instruction. Luke 17:11-19 (RSV) describes ten men with leprosy who were healed by Jesus, showing divine mercy toward the excluded.

leprosy.etymology: From *leprosie*, from Middle French *leprosie* (“leprosy & similar skin diseases”), probably from *leprous* (“leprous”) + *-ie* (“-y”) but possibly from Medieval Latin *leprōsia* (*leprōsus* + *-ia*) although this only historically attested in reference to…

senses.definition: An article of protective clothing that is designed to keep the wearer's head floating above the surface of the water.

core.definition: A buoyant vest worn on the body to keep a person afloat in water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress JAK on the second word, with a lighter stress on life. The last syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'uht'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a safety item and is usually mentioned in serious or instructional contexts, such as boating safety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say life jacket for the vest worn on boats, at pools, or during water sports. Life vest is also common, and boating safety materials often use PFD for personal flotation device. Children and weak swimmers are often told to wear one. The term is used in everyday talk as well as in safety instructions.

distinctions.note: Life vest is very common in American speech and means the same thing, while life jacket is also standard and perhaps slightly more traditional.
PFD is the official term in boating regulations, and it is less common in everyday talk.

examples.everyday: Make sure the kids wear their life jackets before we get in the boat.
examples.professional: Our safety training requires every staff member to check that the life jacket fits before entering the pool area.
examples.analytical: A life jacket is a practical device that embodies a moral principle: it ensures that the vulnerable are held up when the water rises.

nuance.analogy: Like a built-in floating pillow that keeps your head above water even when you stop kicking.
nuance.etymology: Compound of life and jacket, from Old French jaquet, a short coat.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lifejacket' as one word in American writing; two words are standard in American usage.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ket' instead of a reduced 'uht'.

conversation.text: Everyone on the boat has to wear a life jacket.
Do they have life jackets in kids' sizes?
Put your life jacket on before you get in the kayak.

senses.definition: Characterized or marked by litheness; pliant, limber, nimble, lissom.

core.definition: Slender, flexible and graceful in movement; characterized by litheness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the ending as a reduced 'sum' with a schwa. Keep the 'th' voiced, as in 'lithe'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; poetic and somewhat old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'lithesome' in conversation; it appears mainly in poetry, fiction and older prose. Speakers would more often say 'lithe', 'slim' or 'graceful'. Using it in daily talk may sound affected, though it is a pleasant word in writing.

distinctions.note: Lithe is the common, everyday form; lithesome is more poetic and rarer.
Lissome is a close synonym, also literary; both stress graceful suppleness.

examples.everyday: In the old photo, my grandmother looked lithesome, even though she was always tired.
examples.professional: The brochure's lithesome language made the product sound more elegant than it really was.
examples.analytical: The poet's lithesome verse imitates the movement of the dancer it describes.

nuance.analogy: Like a sapling in a breeze, lithesome describes something slender that bends with grace instead of breaking.
nuance.etymology: From lithe plus the suffix -some, meaning 'characterized by'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual conversation where 'lithe' or 'slim' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'lissome' in meaning; they are close, but lissome is somewhat more common in literature.

core.definition: The Gospel miracle in which Jesus feeds a huge crowd with five loaves of bread and two fish; also, material benefits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'FISH'. 'Loaves' ends in a voiced /vz/ and rhymes with 'groves', and 'and' reduces to 'und'. Don't say 'loaf-s'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in the biblical sense of abundance and provision; can be mildly cynical when it means seeking material gain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know the phrase from church and Sunday school. It is used for the miracle, and also in the expression 'loaves and fishes' for the material benefits of a position, often with a hint of criticism. The second use is dated.

distinctions.note: This is the usual title for the miracle; 'loaves and fishes' is shorthand for the same event.
Manna was the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness, a different miracle from the loaves and fishes.
Perks are benefits of a job; 'loaves and fishes' for material gain is older and more literary.

collocations: the miracle of the loaves and fishes

examples.everyday: The kids acted out the loaves and fishes story at Sunday school.
examples.professional: In her sermon on generosity, she used the loaves and fishes to show how God multiplies small offerings.
examples.analytical: The loaves and fishes account shows Jesus both meeting physical need and revealing his identity as the one who provides.

nuance.analogy: It is a small lunch that becomes a feast: a little given freely multiplies.
nuance.etymology: From the English Bible phrase for the bread and fish Jesus multiplied in the Gospel accounts.
common_mistakes: Saying 'loafs' instead of 'loaves'.
Pronouncing 'loaves' as 'lovz' with a short vowel.
Confusing it with the manna miracle.
nuance.biblical_note: All four Gospels tell of Jesus feeding a crowd: Mark 6:30-44, Matthew 14:13-21, Luke 9:10-17 and John 6:1-14. In John 6 a boy offers five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are collected. Mark 8:1-10 and Matthew 15:32-39 record a second feeding of four thousand with seven loaves. John 6 goes on to teach that Jesus is the bread of life.

senses.definition: A type of recurrent neural network (LSTM) with gates that help it remember information over long sequences.

core.definition: A type of recurrent neural network with gates that let it retain information across long sequences, such as text or time series.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MEM in memory, while long, short and term carry secondary stress. The acronym LSTM is usually said as letters, el-es-tee-em, rather than as a word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a precise term in machine learning and AI.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers in the US use the term in papers, code and team meetings, and usually say the acronym LSTM. The phrase is rarely used outside technical settings. When you talk about it, you should say LSTM with each letter spoken, and you can add that it is a kind of recurrent neural network if the listener may not be familiar with it.

distinctions.note: A GRU uses fewer gates and is simpler, while an LSTM has separate input, forget and output gates and a separate cell state.
Short-term memory in psychology refers to human recall over seconds or minutes, while this term is a specific neural network architecture.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says their phone's speech model uses something called an LSTM.
examples.professional: We switched the demand forecasting model to an LSTM so it could capture seasonal patterns across many weeks.
examples.analytical: An LSTM's gates regulate what enters and leaves the cell state, which mitigates vanishing gradients over long sequences.

nuance.analogy: An LSTM is like a notebook with a careful editor who decides what to keep, what to erase and what to read out at each step.
nuance.etymology: Introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997 as a fix for the difficulty recurrent networks have learning long-range dependencies.
common_mistakes: Confusing the technical term with the psychology meaning of short-term memory.
Saying the acronym as a word, like el-stum, instead of spelling it out as el-es-tee-em.

conversation.text: Long short-term memory networks use gates to control what information to keep, forget, and output.
Long short-term memory was introduced in 1997 to address vanishing gradients in recurrent networks.

senses.definition: Pruriently detailed and sensationalistic about something shocking or horrifying, especially with regard to violence or sex.
senses.example: The accident was described with lurid detail.

senses.definition: Melodramatic.
Ghastly, pale, wan in appearance.
Being of a light yellow hue.
senses.example: The lurid lighting of the bar made for a very hazy atmosphere.

senses.definition: Having a brown color tinged with red.

core.definition: Shocking and sensational, often with excessive or unpleasant detail about violence or sex.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The r is pronounced clearly, and the vowel in the second syllable is a short i. Do not say 'LOO-rid.'

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lurid in news writing, reviews, and literary criticism to describe sensational coverage, such as 'lurid details of the crime.' It is a strong, somewhat formal word, so in casual speech people often say 'graphic,' 'gross,' or 'sensational' instead. Calling a color lurid, such as a lurid orange, also means that it is harsh or glaring.

distinctions.note: Graphic describes vivid detail, which can be neutral, while lurid adds a sense of sensationalism and moral excess.
Sensational means designed to excite interest, while lurid is more specifically about shocking or unpleasant detail.

examples.everyday: I stopped reading the article because it was full of lurid details about the accident.
examples.professional: The marketing team cut the lurid language from the ad so it would appeal to families.
examples.analytical: The novel's lurid descriptions of violence raise questions about the moral purpose of sensational fiction.

nuance.analogy: A lurid story is like a flashing neon sign that makes every detail impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin luridus, pale yellow or ghastly.
common_mistakes: Confusing lurid with 'livid,' which means extremely angry.
Using lurid for merely interesting stories; it implies excess or unpleasantness.

senses.definition: A member of the Maccabees (a liberation movement in Israel who established Jewish independence in the Land of Israel in the second and first centuries BCE).

core.definition: The Jewish family and movement led by Judas Maccabeus that revolted against Seleucid rule in the 160s BCE and rededicated the Temple.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the final syllable is a long 'ee' ending in a Z sound. Don't say 'mah-KAH-bees'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; they are remembered as heroic defenders of Jewish faith, though the later Hasmonean dynasty is viewed more critically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet this word mostly in church, Hanukkah discussions, and history or Bible courses. It is plural when naming the movement; 'Maccabee' is one member. 'First and Second Maccabees' are books, not in the Protestant canon.

distinctions.note: Hasmoneans names the dynasty descended from the family, while Maccabees names the revolt and its early leaders.
Zealots were a first-century CE resistance movement against Rome, not the second-century BCE revolt.

examples.everyday: My neighbor explained that Hanukkah celebrates the Maccabees' victory and the rededication of the Temple.
examples.professional: Today's lecture covers the Maccabees and the political world of Judea under the Seleucids.
examples.analytical: The Maccabees' resistance reframed fidelity to the Torah as a political and military obligation, not merely a private devotion.

nuance.analogy: The Maccabees are to Hanukkah what the Founders are to the Fourth of July: a family of rebels at the heart of a national memory.
nuance.etymology: Greek Makkabaios, likely from an Aramaic or Hebrew nickname for Judas, often explained as 'hammer' (maqqebet).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'c' as 'ch' or stressing the second syllable.
Using 'Maccabees' for a single person instead of 'Maccabee'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Maccabees appear in 1 and 2 Maccabees, which are in the Apocrypha (deuterocanonical books), not in the RSV Old Testament proper. 1 Maccabees 4 tells of the cleansing and rededication of the Temple. 2 Maccabees 7 tells of a mother and seven sons who died rather than break the law. 2 Maccabees 12:43-45 is cited in discussions of prayer for the dead.

traditions.view: 1 and 2 Maccabees are canonical deuterocanonical books, and 2 Maccabees 12 is cited in support of prayer for the dead.
1 and 2 Maccabees are received as Scripture, and the Maccabean martyrs are honored as saints; some Orthodox lists also include 3 Maccabees.
The books are not in the canon but are often placed in an Apocrypha section and read for history; Anglicans and Lutherans value them for edification but not for doctrine.

senses.definition: To have enough money to cover expenses; to get by financially; to get through the pay period (sufficient to meet the next payday).

core.definition: To earn or have just enough money to pay for basic living expenses.

pronunciation.tip: The final stress falls on MEET, and the first word has secondary stress. Pronounce the ends with a clear nd and a short e vowel, and do not drop the final s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often sympathetic. It describes financial strain without judgment, though it can sound sad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use make ends meet when talking about money, budgets and living costs, for example after rent goes up. It is common in everyday conversation and news. Do not use it for having large amounts of money; it implies just enough. A natural reply is I know how that is or Hang in there.

distinctions.note: Get by means to manage with difficulty, without necessarily referring to money; make ends meet specifically concerns finances.
Live paycheck to paycheck describes a lifestyle with no savings; make ends meet describes covering basic costs, which may be a near miss.

collocations: make ends meet on a teacher's salary

examples.everyday: With the rent going up again, we're barely making ends meet this month.
examples.professional: Our team is stretched thin, and many junior analysts struggle to make ends meet on the current salary bands.
examples.analytical: Economists measure whether households can make ends meet by comparing income with the cost of necessities, not with discretionary spending.

nuance.analogy: Making ends meet is like stretching a blanket that is just a little too short: you cover what you need, but nothing extra.
nuance.etymology: Ends here means the two sides of a budget, income and expenses; meet means to come together and balance.
common_mistakes: Saying meet the ends, with the wrong word order.
Using it to mean being wealthy; it means having just enough to cover costs.

conversation.text: A lot of families work two jobs just to make ends meet.
When I was in grad school, I tutored on weekends to make ends meet.
It's hard to make ends meet with rent this high.

senses.definition: An official or authoritative command; an order or injunction; a commission; a judicial precept; an authorization.
The order or authority to do something, as granted to a politician by the electorate.
A period during which a government is in power.
(historical) An order by the League of Nations to a member nation to establish a government responsible for a conquered territory, as the colonies of Germany after World War I.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Such a territory.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To (officially) require someone to do something or act in a certain way, to give them the authority to do so; to command.
To make mandatory.
To administer or assign a territory to a nation under a mandate. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: An official order or authority, especially the approval voters give a government to carry out a particular policy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second vowel is a long ay, and the final t is a clear sound, not silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal; it can sound heavy when used for government power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mandate most often for a government's claimed authority after an election, as in 'a mandate for change,' or for required rules, as in 'a vaccine mandate.' In casual speech, requirement or rule is more natural, since mandate sounds official or political.

distinctions.note: An order is a direct instruction from one person, while a mandate is authority given by a larger body such as voters or a legislature.
A requirement is any condition that must be met, while a mandate is an official directive, often from a higher authority.

examples.everyday: My landlord says the new mandate means we have to get our smoke detectors checked.
examples.professional: The compliance team reviewed the new data-retention mandate before the audit.
examples.analytical: A government's claim to a mandate rests on whether voters actually authorized its specific policies, not just its general victory.

nuance.analogy: A mandate is like a permission slip signed by the people, which lets an official act on their behalf.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mandatum, 'something entrusted,' from mandare, to entrust or order.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in man-DATE.
Confusing mandate with demand; a mandate carries official authority, not just a request.

mandate.etymology: Latin *mandātum* (“a charge, order, command, commission, injunction”), substantivized from the neuter forms of *mandātus*, perfect passive participle of *mandō* (“to commit to one's charge, order, command, commission, literally to put into one's hands”)…

senses.definition: One who willingly accepts being put to death or willingly accepts challenging and exposing iniquity done to oneself for adhering openly to one's religious beliefs; notably, saints canonized after red martyrdom.
senses.example: The apostle Stephen was the first Christian martyr.

senses.definition: One who sacrifices their life, station, or something of great personal value, for the sake of principle or to sustain a cause.
One who suffers greatly or constantly, even involuntarily.
senses.example: Stan is a martyr to arthritis, Chris is a martyr to Stan's endless moaning about it.

senses.definition: Someone who exaggerates their pain and suffering in order to gain sympathy.
senses.example: You have a great life! Stop trying to play the martyr!

senses.definition: To make someone into a martyr by putting them to death for adhering to, or acting in accordance with, some belief, especially religious; to sacrifice on account of faith or profession.
To persecute.
senses.example: Some religious and other minorities were martyred until extinction.

senses.definition: To torment; to torture.

core.definition: A person who dies or suffers greatly for refusing to give up their religious beliefs or a cause they strongly believe in.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced, rhotic schwa-like sound, so do not add a full 'tor' vowel; the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or respectful when describing people who died for principle, but it can be negative or mocking when someone plays the martyr for attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use martyr in serious contexts about history and faith, and in casual speech about people who complain loudly about sacrifices. Saying someone 'is being a martyr' suggests they want sympathy, which can sound a bit teasing. A natural reply to 'I'll do the dishes, it's fine' might be 'Don't be a martyr, let me help.'

distinctions.note: A hero is admired for courage in general, while a martyr specifically suffers or dies for a principle or faith.
A victim is harmed by something, often without choice, while a martyr willingly accepts suffering for a cause.

examples.everyday: Stop playing the martyr, you can just tell me you want the last slice of pizza.
examples.professional: Our product lead was a martyr to the launch schedule, working every weekend for six months and never asking for help.
examples.analytical: The early church revered Stephen as the first martyr because he bore witness to Christ even as he was stoned.

nuance.analogy: A martyr is like a lighthouse keeper who stays at the post through the storm, refusing to leave even when it costs everything.
nuance.etymology: From Greek martys, meaning witness.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in mar-TYR.
Using martyr for anyone who is simply tired or upset, rather than someone who sacrifices for a cause.

martyr.etymology: From Middle English *martir*, from Old English *martyr*, itself a borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin *martyr*, from Ancient Greek *μάρτυρ*, later form of *μάρτυς* (“witness”).

core.definition: An ancient town in the tableland east of the Jordan River, in Moab's territory, later assigned to Reuben and known today as Madaba in Jordan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MED. The middle syllable is a short 'uh,' and the final vowel is a soft 'uh,' not 'ee' or 'ay.' Do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name from Scripture and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Medeba' mostly in Bible study, biblical geography, and archaeology. In modern conversation, people usually say 'Madaba' for the town in Jordan. If you mention Medeba in a church discussion, a quick note that it is the same place as Madaba helps.

distinctions.note: Medeba is the biblical name; Madaba is the modern Jordanian name for the same town, often used in archaeology and travel.

examples.everyday: We visited Madaba in Jordan, and the guide said it was the old Medeba from the Bible.
examples.professional: In the lesson on Israelite geography, I show students where Medeba sat on the map near the border with Moab.
examples.analytical: The mention of Medeba in Numbers 21:30 and Isaiah 15:2 helps scholars locate the Moabite and Israelite frontier in the Transjordan.

nuance.analogy: Medeba is like an old street name that still appears on maps even after the city renamed it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Mêdeva; the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Medeba with Mede, the people of Media.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'meh-DEE-buh.'
nuance.biblical_note: Medeba is a town in the Transjordan that appears in the story of Israel's wars and borders. Numbers 21:30 mentions Medeba in the context of the conquest of Sihon's territory, which involved the Amorites and Moab. Joshua 13:9 and 13:16 place it in the tribal land of Reuben, and Isaiah 15:2 includes it in an oracle of mourning over Moab.

senses.definition: A keepsake; an object kept as a reminder of a place or event.
senses.example: I kept the shell as a memento of my visit to the seashore.

core.definition: A small object you keep to remember a special place, event or person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MEN, and the first and last syllables are weak. The final vowel is a long 'oh', not 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'memento' in everyday speech for a keepsake from a trip, party or event, such as a ticket stub or a small souvenir. It sounds warm and slightly sentimental, so it fits well with a gift or a photo album. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I'll keep it as a memento.'

distinctions.note: A souvenir is bought or picked up as a reminder of a trip, while a memento can be any object kept because it carries personal meaning.
Keepsake is a near-synonym that sounds more homey, while memento sounds slightly more formal or reflective.

examples.everyday: I brought you this seashell as a memento from our beach trip.
examples.professional: The company gave each retiring employee a small plaque as a memento of their years of service.
examples.analytical: For the narrator, the letter functions as a memento that anchors a past she can no longer fully reach.

nuance.analogy: A memento is like a pressed flower in a book: small, quiet, and holding a whole moment inside it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin memento, the imperative of meminisse, meaning remember.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'men' with a long vowel or stressing the last syllable.
Using 'memento' for a receipt or document that has no personal meaning.

memento.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *mementō* (“remember”), imperative form of *meminī* (“to remember”).

senses.definition: A collection of live wild animals as an exhibition historically associated with the aristocracy and considered a precursor of modern zoos.
The enclosure where they are kept.
A diverse or miscellaneous group.
The orchestra of a theater.

core.definition: A collection of wild or exotic animals kept for display; also, any varied or odd group of people or things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAJ. The final "-ie" is pronounced "ree", and the middle "-er-" is a reduced "uh".

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use menagerie for animal collections in parks or private homes, and often in a playful way for a group of odd or quirky people. Saying "This office is a menagerie" is a friendly comment. It sounds old-fashioned for a modern zoo, where Americans usually say zoo.

distinctions.note: A zoo is a modern, organized public institution; a menagerie is an older or informal collection of animals.
Collection is neutral and general; menagerie suggests a varied, sometimes chaotic mix of creatures or people.

examples.everyday: My sister's house is a menagerie with two dogs, a cat, and three fish.
examples.professional: Our team is a menagerie of backgrounds, from statisticians to former designers, which keeps our meetings interesting.
examples.analytical: Early modern European courts maintained royal menageries as displays of power, which later evolved into public zoos.

nuance.analogy: A menagerie is like a box of mixed crayons: many different colors and types, all gathered in one place.
nuance.etymology: From French ménagerie, from ménage, household, from Latin mansio-related roots.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable.
Using menagerie as a synonym for zoo in formal American writing; zoo is the standard term.

menagerie.etymology: From French *ménagerie*, derived from *ménager* (“to keep house”), *ménage*.

senses.definition: A mindset; a way of thinking; a set of beliefs.
senses.example: Before he can succeed, he will have to shed the mentality that he can get by without hard work.

senses.definition: The characteristics of a mind described as a system of distinctive structures and processes based in biology, language, or culture, etc. a mental system.

core.definition: A habitual way of thinking; a set of attitudes and beliefs that shapes how someone sees situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAL. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the final 'ity' is pronounced 'uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral by default; it becomes negative with words like 'siege mentality' or 'us-versus-them mentality'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mentality' often in business, sports, politics, and everyday discussion of attitudes, as in 'a winning mentality'. It is neutral but can sound critical when it describes a narrow or fixed way of thinking. 'Mindset' is a close and very common American alternative.

distinctions.note: Mindset is the more common American word in business and self-help talk. Mentality is slightly more formal and can carry a stronger sense of group attitude.
Attitude is a feeling or position toward something in a particular moment. Mentality is deeper and more habitual.

examples.everyday: My coach says we need a winning mentality if we want to beat that team.
examples.professional: Our product team needs a customer-first mentality when we plan the next release.
examples.analytical: Weber traced how a religious mentality shaped the economic habits of early capitalism.

nuance.analogy: A mentality is like the default setting on a computer: it runs in the background and shapes what happens next.
nuance.etymology: From French mentalité, from Medieval Latin mentalitas, from mentalis, mental.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'mental', the adjective. You can say 'a mental state' but 'a state of mentality' sounds unusual.
Using it for simple thoughts. It refers to a habitual pattern, not one idea.

senses.definition: That is the ratio of two holomorphic functions (and so possibly infinite at a discrete set of points).

core.definition: Of a complex function: holomorphic everywhere except at isolated poles, so it can be written as a ratio of two holomorphic functions.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MOR, in the middle of the word, and the 'o' in 'mero' is a diphthong 'oh'. Keep the r clear in both syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in complex analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meromorphic' only in mathematics, especially complex analysis and graduate courses. In conversation, mathematicians would say 'a function with poles' or 'holomorphic except at poles' when they want a plainer phrase. Outside technical settings, the word would sound very specialized.

distinctions.note: A holomorphic function is complex differentiable at every point of its domain; a meromorphic function may fail to be holomorphic at isolated poles.
Analytic is a broader term in complex analysis; meromorphic specifically allows isolated poles.

examples.everyday: My math homework asked whether a certain function was meromorphic, and I still am not sure what that means.
examples.professional: The simulation model assumes the transfer function is meromorphic, so its poles determine the system's stability.
examples.analytical: A function that is meromorphic on the whole complex plane can be expressed as a quotient of entire functions, which clarifies the role of its poles.

nuance.analogy: Like a smooth road with a few potholes that are isolated and countable: the road is mostly fine, but the holes are places where it breaks.
nuance.etymology: From Greek meros, 'part', and morphē, 'form', with the -ic suffix; the term refers to functions that are mostly holomorphic.
common_mistakes: Confusing meromorphic with 'homomorphic', which is a term from algebra.
Forgetting that poles are isolated points, not whole regions where the function fails.

core.definition: A member of the Midianites, a nomadic desert people descended from Abraham through his son Midian, who appear in the Old Testament as traders and enemies of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MID. The middle syllable is a weak 'ee-uh', and the final syllable rhymes with 'bite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a term used in Bible study and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Midianite mainly in Bible classes, sermons and scholarly discussion of the Old Testament. It can be a noun for a person or an adjective, as in 'the Midianite traders.' It is not used in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Midian is the name of the ancestor and the region; Midianite refers to the people who lived there.

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned the Midianites in last Sunday's sermon, and I looked them up afterward.
examples.professional: For the lesson plan, students should compare how the Midianite traders appear in Genesis and in the story of Gideon.
examples.analytical: The Midianite identity in the Hebrew Bible is shaped by the tension between kinship with Israel and their role as enemies, a tension the text handles with care.

nuance.analogy: The Midianites are like a neighboring family in a long feud and a long friendship at once: close enough to be related, but often on the other side of the fence.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Midyan, the name of Abraham's son, with the suffix -ite meaning a member of a group.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'mid-ee-AN-ite'; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Using Midianite as a word for any desert nomad; it refers to a specific people in the Bible.
nuance.biblical_note: The Midianites were a people descended from Abraham through Midian, appearing in the Old Testament as traders, herders and raiders. In Genesis 37:28 RSV, Midianite traders draw Joseph out of the pit and he is sold to Ishmaelites who carry him to Egypt, and in Genesis 37:36 the Midianites sell him in Egypt. In Numbers 31 RSV, Israel makes war on the Midianites, and in Judges 6-8 RSV, Gideon defeats Midianite raiders who had oppressed Israel. The Midianites are also mentioned as part of the wider network of desert peoples around Israel.

senses.definition: To toil, to work hard.
To churn continually; to swirl.
To defile or dirty.
Hard work.
Confusion, turmoil.
A spot; a defilement.
The glass circling the tip of a blowpipe or punty, such as the residual glass after detaching a blown vessel, or the lower part of a gather.

The excess material which adheres to the top, base, or rim of a glass object when it is cut or knocked off from a blowpipe or punty, or from the mold-filling process. Typically removed after annealing as part of the finishing process (e.g. scored and snapped off).
The metallic oxide from a blowpipe which has adhered to a glass object.

core.definition: Working hard and persistently at tiring, unpleasant labor. Also, churning or stirring continually.

pronunciation.tip: The word is "moil" with the vowel of "boy," plus "-ing." Stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It suggests exhausting, grinding toil, often with a sense of being overwhelmed.
nuance.usage_note: "Moiling" is a literary word. Americans are more likely to say "toiling," "slaving away," or "working like crazy" in ordinary speech. You may see it in older novels, poetry, or formal essays about hard labor. It is rare enough that a native speaker may need a moment to recognize it.

distinctions.note: "Toiling" is the common everyday word for hard, sustained work. "Moiling" sounds more literary and emphasizes the messiness or drudgery.

distinctions.vs: moiling in the sense of churning
distinctions.note: Both senses come from the same root, but the labor sense is far more common in modern English.

examples.everyday: After the storm, we were moiling in the basement all afternoon, pumping water out.
examples.professional: The team has been moiling over the legacy code for weeks, trying to fix a bug nobody understands.
examples.analytical: The novelist describes the peasants moiling in the fields, and this image of endless labor frames the whole moral argument of the book.

nuance.analogy: Moiling is like a stick stirring thick mud: constant, exhausting motion that never gets anywhere clean.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English "moilen," meaning to make wet or dirty, from Old French "moillier," to wet or soften.
common_mistakes: Using "moiling" in casual conversation, where "working hard" would sound more natural.
Giving it a "w" sound at the start, which is incorrect for this word.

senses.definition: To be overprotective and indulgent toward; to pamper.
(rare) A person, especially a man or a boy, who is pampered and overprotected.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To treat someone too gently or protectively, doing things for them that they should learn to do themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable MAH and the second syllable KAH. The final syllables are reduced, so the last two sound like 'dul', not 'dawl'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that the person being coddled is weak or immature, and that the protection is harmful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mollycoddle informally, often for parents, teachers, or bosses who protect people too much. It is often used with a judgment, as in 'Stop mollycoddling him.' It can sound harsh if said directly to someone, so people often use it when talking about a third person. A natural reply is 'You're right, I need to let him figure it out.'

distinctions.note: Pamper means to indulge someone with comfort or luxury and can be positive, while mollycoddle is always critical of overprotection.
Coddle is the same kind of gentle indulgence but is milder and can be affectionate, while mollycoddle is stronger and more disapproving.

examples.everyday: Stop mollycoddling your little brother, he is old enough to tie his own shoes.
examples.professional: We should not mollycoddle junior analysts, because they learn faster when they debug their own code.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that an overly protective welfare system can mollycoddle citizens and weaken their sense of responsibility.

nuance.analogy: To mollycoddle someone is like wrapping a young plant in so much cloth that it never grows strong roots.
nuance.etymology: Nineteenth-century English, combining 'molly' (an effeminate man or boy) with 'coddle' (to pamper).
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'molly coddle' with two words in formal writing.
Using it as a neutral word for gentle care; it is usually critical.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: A set of moral norms or customs derived from generally accepted practices rather than written laws.

core.definition: The customs and moral standards that a particular society or group takes for granted as right and proper.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'days'. The word is a plural noun, but Americans use it with singular verbs in many contexts, though it is usually treated as plural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Mores is used mainly in sociology, history, ethics, and formal writing when describing a group's unwritten rules. Americans say it in serious discussion about cultural change, such as shifting social mores. In casual speech, people more often say customs, values, or norms.

distinctions.note: Norms is more general and often used in social science; mores implies deeper moral weight and is more closely tied to what is considered right.
Laws are written and enforced by the state; mores are unwritten and enforced by social approval or disapproval.

examples.everyday: Some of the old dating mores in our town seem strange to my kids now.
examples.professional: Our HR training covers the workplace mores that new hires may not know, such as how to address senior staff.
examples.analytical: Durkheim argues that a society's mores are internalized through education and ritual, which makes them more binding than law.

nuance.analogy: Mores are like the unwritten house rules of a whole society: nobody posted them on the fridge, but everyone knows when someone breaks one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mores, plural of mos, meaning custom or manner.
common_mistakes: Using mores as a singular noun, as in 'a more' for one rule.
Confusing mores with the comparative 'more' in pronunciation or meaning.

mores.etymology: From Latin *mōrēs* (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of *mōs*.

core.definition: A person who feels responsible for the well-being of others, especially those in need. The phrase comes from Cain's question in the Bible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRUH and KEE. The 'th' in 'brother' is voiced, as in 'the,' and the final 'er' is a reduced American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing care for others, but can be negative when used to reject responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in sermons, speeches, community talk and everyday conversation about helping others. It sounds slightly formal or literary, and it often appears in the negative form 'I am not my brother's keeper' to deny responsibility. Use it with care in mixed company, because many Americans will recognize the biblical source.

distinctions.note: A good Samaritan is a person who helps a stranger in need, while 'my brother's keeper' describes a broader sense of responsibility for others.
'Responsible for' is a plain and neutral phrase, while 'my brother's keeper' carries a moral and religious tone.

examples.everyday: When my friend lost her job, I felt like I had to be her brother's keeper and help her find work.
examples.professional: As a team lead, I see myself as my brother's keeper, so I check in when someone is overloaded.
examples.analytical: Cain's reply in Genesis 4:9 raises the question of whether moral responsibility extends beyond kinship to all neighbors.

nuance.analogy: It is like a shared lifeboat: each person in it is responsible for keeping the others afloat.
nuance.etymology: Derived from the biblical question in Genesis 4:9, in the Revised Standard Version wording 'Am I my brother's keeper?'
common_mistakes: Using 'my brother's keeper' only for a sibling; the phrase refers to any fellow human being.
Confusing 'keeper' with a goalkeeper or zookeeper; here 'keeper' means someone who guards or looks after someone.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'keeper' is shomer, meaning guard or watchman, from the root shamar, meaning to keep, guard or watch. In Genesis 4:9 Cain responds to God's question about Abel with 'Am I my brother's keeper?', which is a question that denies responsibility and hides his guilt. God answers by hearing Abel's blood crying from the ground in Genesis 4:10, which shows that Abel's fate matters to God. Genesis 4:12 then shows the consequences for Cain, who becomes a fugitive and wanderer.

senses.definition: A proposition which is the contradictory of another proposition and which can be obtained from that other proposition by the appropriately placed addition, or insertion, of the word "not". (Or, in symbolic logic, by prepending that proposition with the symbol for the logical operator "not".)
The logical operation which obtains such (negated) propositions.
The act of negating something.
A denial or contradiction.
A negative particle; a word, particularly an adverb, with a negative meaning: for instance, no and not in English, nōn, haud and nē in Latin, οὐ and μή in ancient Greek.

core.definition: In logic, a statement that says the opposite of another statement, often formed by adding 'not'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'GAY', and the final syllable 'shun' is reduced to a syllabic n, so it is 'nih-GAY-shn'. Don't pronounce a full vowel after the sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in logic, mathematics, and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'negation' mainly in logic, mathematics, grammar, and philosophy classes, and it is standard in those fields. In everyday talk the word is rare; people say 'the opposite' or 'not'. In grammar, 'negation' refers to words like 'not' and 'never' that make a sentence negative.

distinctions.note: 'Negative' is a general adjective, while 'negation' is the logical or grammatical operation of making something negative.
'Denial' is a social or emotional refusal to accept a fact, while 'negation' is a neutral logical operation.

examples.everyday: My kid's English homework was about negation, so we practiced making sentences with 'not' and 'never'.
examples.professional: In the SQL query, the negation of the condition excludes every row where the status is active.
examples.analytical: In classical logic, the negation of a proposition is true exactly when the proposition is false, which is the basis of proof by contradiction.

nuance.analogy: Negation is like a mirror in logic: it flips a statement to its opposite while keeping its structure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'negatio', from 'negare', meaning to deny or say no.
common_mistakes: Using 'negation' in everyday conversation where 'the opposite' would be more natural.
Confusing 'negation' with 'negative'; the noun names the operation, while the adjective describes the result.
patterns: [U, C] the negation of a statement

negation.etymology: From Middle English *negacioun*, from Old French *negacion*, from Latin *negātiō* (“a denial; negative word”).

senses.definition: Within a topological space:
Within a metric space:
The infinitesimal open set of all points that may be reached directly from a given point.
The set of all the vertices adjacent to a given vertex.
The residential area near one's home.
senses.example: He lives in my neighborhood.

senses.definition: The inhabitants of a residential area.
senses.example: The fire alarmed the neighborhood.

senses.definition: A formal or informal division of a municipality or region.
senses.example: We have just moved to a pleasant neighborhood.

senses.definition: An approximate amount.
senses.example: He must be making in the neighborhood of $200,000 per year.

senses.definition: The quality of physical proximity.
senses.example: The slums and the palace were in awful neighborhood.

senses.definition: A set containing an open set which contains some specified point.
Alternatively: An open set which contains some specified point.
A set containing an open ball which contains a specified point.
Alternatively: An open ball which contains some specified point.
The set of all cells near a given cell used to determine that cell's state in the next generation.
(dated) Close proximity; nearness.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A local area within a town or city, or the people who live there.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick, weak 'bur,' and the final 'hood' rhymes with 'good.'

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting community and familiarity, though it can imply safety or danger depending on the area.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neighborhood constantly for local areas, such as 'a quiet neighborhood' or 'what's the neighborhood like?' It can describe a specific area of a city, a suburb, or a group of neighbors. In math, the word has a precise technical meaning.

distinctions.note: Community emphasizes shared identity or interests and may not be geographic, while neighborhood is a specific local area.
A district is an official or administrative area, while a neighborhood is an informal, lived-in area.

examples.everyday: We moved to a quieter neighborhood near the park, and the kids can ride bikes on the sidewalk.
examples.professional: The data team is mapping service requests by neighborhood to find where response times are longest.
examples.analytical: In a metric space, a neighborhood of a point is an open set containing that point, which lets us define limits without fixing a distance.

nuance.analogy: A neighborhood is like a ring of nearby houses around your own: everything you can reach easily from your front door.
nuance.etymology: From neighbor plus -hood, a suffix meaning 'condition or group,' so 'the state of being neighbors.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a full 'bor' rather than a weak 'bur.'
Using neighborhood to mean a single house; it refers to a wider area.

neighborhood.etymology: From an alteration of earlier *neighborred* (“neighborhood”), from Middle English *neȝeburredde*, *neheborreden*, equivalent to *neighbor* + *red*; the term being interpreted as *neighbor* + *-hood*.

conversation.text: Is this a safe neighborhood to walk around at night?
Our neighborhood has a great bakery and a park.
Slow down; this is a neighborhood with lots of kids.

senses.definition: Said in response to an obvious statement.
senses.example: Person A: The Cleveland Browns are not doing too awful well this year.

senses.definition: An exclamation of amazement.

core.definition: An informal exclamation meaning you agree strongly, or that you are surprised or impressed by what someone said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KID, and the -ing ending is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ing' rather than 'eeng'. Link the two words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lighthearted; it can express agreement, sarcasm, or real surprise depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it casually among friends or colleagues, often as 'No kidding!' to show that an obvious point is obvious or that a surprise is genuine. Tone matters: said flatly after an obvious statement, it can sound sarcastic. Avoid it in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Really? asks for confirmation; no kidding expresses agreement or surprise and does not expect an answer.
You don't say is a little more ironic and older-sounding; no kidding is more casual and common.

examples.everyday: It's supposed to hit ninety degrees today. No kidding, it's brutal out there.
examples.professional: The migration failed twice before it worked. No kidding, we were all surprised.
examples.analytical: When a conclusion is trivially obvious, the reply no kidding can reveal how little the speaker expected of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like saying 'you think?' with a grin: it confirms the obvious with a little humor.
common_mistakes: Using it as a literal question about kids, which confuses learners; it means 'really' or 'I agree'.
Using it in formal writing or serious discussion, where it sounds too casual.

conversation.text: "It's really hot today." "No kidding. It's like a hundred degrees."
"I used to live in your building." "No kidding! Which floor?"
"This line is long." "No kidding. We've been here forever."

senses.definition: Describes inputs unlike anything in the training data, where a model's behavior is unreliable.

core.definition: Describing data or inputs that differ from the examples a machine learning model was trained on, so its predictions may be unreliable.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on BYOO, in "distribution." The flapped t in "distribution" sounds like a soft d, and "of" reduces to "uhv."

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a warning that a model is working outside its experience.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers use this term in model evaluation, monitoring, and safety discussions. It is nearly always used before a noun, such as "out-of-distribution inputs." In a meeting, a natural phrase is "We need to test for out-of-distribution cases before launch."

distinctions.note: Out-of-sample usually means data held out from training but drawn from the same distribution. Out-of-distribution means data that comes from a different distribution entirely.
An anomaly is an unusual data point, often within the normal data range. Out-of-distribution input is defined by its relation to the training distribution.

examples.everyday: The app worked fine on the sample photos, but it failed on pictures taken at night, which were out-of-distribution.
examples.professional: Before deploying the model, let's run out-of-distribution tests on the new regional data.
examples.analytical: A model's confidence on out-of-distribution inputs is often misleading, since it extrapolates patterns it never learned.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver trained only on city roads who suddenly faces a mountain highway, a model performs unpredictably on terrain it never trained on.
common_mistakes: Writing "out of distribution" without hyphens before a noun.
Confusing it with "out-of-sample," which refers to held-out data from the same source.
Stressing "DIS-tri-bu-tion" instead of the correct stress on BYOO.

conversation.text: The model is overconfident on out-of-distribution inputs, such as photos taken at night.
We need an out-of-distribution detector that flags inputs the model wasn't trained to handle.

senses.definition: To bring about the downfall of (a government, etc.), especially by force; to usurp.
senses.example: I hate the current government, but not enough to want to overthrow them.

senses.definition: To throw (something) so that it goes too far.
senses.example: He overthrew first base, for an error.

senses.definition: (rare) To throw down to the ground, to overturn.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A removal, especially of a ruler or government, by force or threat of force; usurpation.
A throw that goes too far.
senses.example: He overthrew the ball and it went for four runs.

senses.definition: A run scored by the batting side when a fielder throws the ball back to the infield, whence it continues to the opposite outfield.

core.definition: To remove a ruler or government from power, usually by force or a sudden political action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on throw, the second syllable of the word. The th is voiceless, and the r after th is a light American r sound, not a trill.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, because it describes the removal of power, often by violence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overthrow in news, history and politics, as in 'rebels tried to overthrow the government.' In sports, a baseball overthrow is a throw that goes too far, which is very common in American conversation. Casual speakers may say 'toppled' or 'ousted,' but overthrow is a natural word.

distinctions.note: Topple is a more physical or informal word, suggesting something falling down; overthrow is more formal and political.
Oust means to force someone out of a position, often without violence; overthrow usually involves a government being removed by force.

examples.everyday: Movies love stories about a hero who overthrows a corrupt king.
examples.professional: The team tried to overthrow the old scoring model, but leadership kept it for now.
examples.analytical: Political theorists debate whether a people has a right to overthrow a government that systematically violates its rights.

nuance.analogy: Like knocking over a chess king: the ruler is toppled from the top of the power structure.
nuance.etymology: From Old English oferþrāwan, from ofer (over) and þrāwan (to twist, turn).
common_mistakes: Confusing overthrow with overturn; overturn often refers to decisions or laws, while overthrow refers to ruling power.
Using overthrow for a simple disagreement; it implies removing power, often by force.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 19:25 the LORD overthrows the cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, as a judgment. In Acts 5:38-39 Gamaliel warns the council that if the movement is of God, they will not be able to overthrow it. The RSV uses overthrow for the act of destroying or ending something by a powerful force, whether divine judgment or human opposition.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a paradigm.
Related as members of a substitution class.
(historical) A writer of memoirs of religious persons, as examples of Christian excellence.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Relating to a paradigm, meaning a clear model or framework that serves as a pattern for thinking or practice.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -MAT- syllable, not on the first syllable. The -ig- is often weakened to a short 'ih' sound, so say 'dig' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a structure or model without praising or criticizing it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic, scientific and philosophical writing, often with 'shift' (a paradigmatic shift). In everyday speech people say 'model' or 'framework' instead. In linguistics it describes relations between words that can substitute for each other, which is a different sense from the everyday one.

distinctions.note: A paradigm is the noun for a model or framework; paradigmatic is the adjective describing something that belongs to, or is typical of, such a model.
Exemplary praises something as a good example to imitate; paradigmatic only means it serves as a model, without judging its quality.

examples.everyday: Her move to a smaller town is a paradigmatic case of someone trading career ambition for quality of life.
examples.professional: Moving the team from monthly releases to continuous deployment was a paradigmatic shift in how we build software.
examples.analytical: Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions treats the replacement of Ptolemaic astronomy as a paradigmatic case of theory change.

nuance.analogy: A paradigmatic example is like a textbook diagram: it shows the whole pattern clearly enough that you can recognize every other case.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin paradigma, from Greek paradeigma, 'pattern, model', from paradeiknunai, 'to show side by side'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'par-uh-DIG-muh-tik'.
Using paradigmatic to mean simply 'typical' in casual talk, where 'classic' or 'textbook' is more natural.

senses.definition: The doctrine that matter and mind do not causally interact but that physiological events in the brain or body nonetheless occur simultaneously with matching events in the mind.
The use of parallel methods in hardware or software, so that several tasks can be performed at the same time.
The state or condition of being parallel; agreement in direction, tendency, or character.
The state of being in agreement or similarity; resemblance, correspondence, analogy.
A parallel position; the relation of parallels.
The juxtaposition of two or more identical or equivalent syntactic constructions, especially those expressing the same sentiment with slight modifications, introduced for rhetorical effect.
In antitrust law, the practice of competitors of raising prices by roughly the same amount at roughly the same time, without engaging in a formal agreement to do so.
Similarity of features between two species resulting from their having taken similar evolutionary paths following their initial divergence from a common ancestor.

core.definition: The quality of being parallel, or close similarity in structure, direction or character between things; in computing, doing many calculations at the same time, for example across several processors or GPUs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAIR. The ending '-ism' is reduced to 'iz-um', and the word has four syllables, not five.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a structural correspondence, often admired in writing and design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'parallelism' mainly in academic or technical settings. In a workplace, it may refer to parallel processing or parallel development ('parallelism in our testing environments'). In writing, it describes matching grammatical structures, and in Bible study it refers to the balance of poetic lines.

distinctions.note: Parallel is a common adjective or noun for lines or things that run side by side; parallelism is the abstract quality of such correspondence.
Similarity means that things look or work alike; parallelism means they match in structure or direction over time or in parallel.

examples.everyday: That speech had a nice parallelism to it, with each sentence starting the same way.
examples.professional: We need better parallelism between the staging and production environments so our tests mean something.
examples.analytical: Psalm 19:1 shows synonymous parallelism, where the second line restates the first in different words.

nuance.analogy: Parallelism is like two railway tracks: they run side by side, matching in direction and spacing, so the whole route stays aligned.
nuance.etymology: From parallel, from Greek parallēlos, 'alongside one another', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in 'par-uh-lel-iz-um' with a separate 'ell' sound.
Using parallelism only for lines in geometry; in writing and poetry it describes matching structure.
nuance.biblical_note: There is no single Hebrew term for parallelism; it is a scholarly label for the structure of much Hebrew poetry, where lines correspond to one another. Key passages: Psalm 19:1 has the heavens and the firmament repeating the same idea in parallel lines. Proverbs 10:1 offers a contrast between the wise son and the foolish son, a form called antithetic parallelism. Psalm 24:1 states that the earth belongs to the LORD in a pattern of repeated lines.

senses.definition: A work or performance that imitates another work or performance with ridicule or irony.
To make a parody of something.
senses.example: The comedy movie parodied the entire Western genre.

core.definition: A humorous imitation of a work, style, or person that exaggerates it to mock or comment on it; to make such an imitation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the word ends in a long ee sound, not -ij. The first vowel is the vowel of cat in many American accents, though pair is also common.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually signals playful or sharp humor, though a parody can also be a mocking criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parody for film, TV, music, and books, for example a comedy that spoofs a famous movie. The informal equivalent is spoof. Calling something a parody is generally a compliment to its wit, but it can be an insult if the work is seen as empty imitation.

distinctions.note: Satire criticizes society or people through humor; parody specifically imitates a particular work or style.
Spoof is a lighter, more informal word for a comic imitation; parody can be more literary or sharp.

examples.everyday: Have you seen that parody of the old cop show? It is hilarious.
examples.professional: Our marketing video was a parody of corporate training videos, and leadership liked it.
examples.analytical: Cervantes's novel works as a parody of chivalric romance, exposing its conventions through exaggeration.

nuance.analogy: A parody is like a funhouse mirror: it reflects the original accurately in shape but stretches it for laughs.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parodia, a song sung alongside another, from para, beside, and ode, song.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as -ij, as in the dictionary transcription; it is -dee.
Using parody to mean any kind of joke, when it specifically means imitation of a particular work or style.

parody.etymology: From Latin *parōdia*, from Ancient Greek *παρῳδία* (“parody”), from *παρά* (“besides”) + *ᾠδή* (“song”).

senses.definition: An exclusive focus on a particular area, group, sect, etc.
The principle that only certain people are chosen by God for salvation.
The principle that individual states, races of a federation, etc. may act independently of a central authority.

core.definition: An exclusive attachment to one group, region, or tradition, placing its particular interests above universal principles.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TIK, the second syllable. The -cular- part reduces to 'kyuh-lur', and the final -ism is a short 'iz-um'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, suggesting narrowness or favoritism, though it can be neutral in philosophy or political science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use particularism mainly in philosophy, political theory, religious studies, and history, rarely in everyday talk. It's often used critically: 'a particularism that undermines universal rights.' In everyday speech, 'tribalism' or 'favoritism' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Parochialism is narrow-mindedness about local concerns; particularism is more often a philosophical or theological position about priorities.
Universalism holds that principles or salvation apply to all; particularism holds that they are restricted to certain groups.

examples.everyday: My uncle's particularism makes it hard to talk about other cities, because he thinks only our town really matters.
examples.professional: Leadership needs to avoid particularism in hiring, so that the criteria apply the same way to every department.
examples.analytical: Ethical particularism challenges the view that moral judgments must follow general rules, arguing that good judgment responds to the unique features of each case.

nuance.analogy: Particularism is like a family that trusts only its own relatives, ignoring the principles that should apply to everyone.
nuance.etymology: From particular plus -ism, from Latin particularis, 'of a part.'
common_mistakes: Confusing particularism with particularity, which means specificity or a distinctive feature.
Pronouncing the middle -cu- as 'kyoo' too strongly; it's usually 'kyuh'.
Using it as a synonym for 'particular detail'.

senses.definition: Very enthusiastic about something.

core.definition: Caring a great deal about something and feeling strong enthusiasm for it in your daily life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PASH and BOWT. The about is reduced to uh-BOWT, but keep the t crisp; in fast speech the phrase sounds like PASH-uh-nit-uh-BOWT.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly, and a natural way to show interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask 'What are you passionate about?' at parties, networking events, and first meetings. Answer with a specific topic, such as 'I'm passionate about hiking in the mountains.' A natural follow-up reply is 'Oh, that's great, how did you get into it?'

distinctions.note: Interested in is weaker and neutral, while passionate about shows much deeper enthusiasm.
Into is very casual and common in speech, as in I'm into hiking, while passionate about sounds more heartfelt.

examples.everyday: What are you passionate about outside of work? I'm passionate about rock climbing.
examples.professional: I'm passionate about building data pipelines that people actually trust, so I'd love to lead that project.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers are passionate about questions of meaning, yet they rarely agree on how such passion should be justified.

nuance.analogy: Like a cause you would happily argue for at dinner, with no need to be asked twice.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective passionate, from Late Latin passionatus.
common_mistakes: Saying passionate of instead of passionate about.
Overusing it in formal emails where a plainer phrase would be better.
Stressing about, saying passionate uh-BOWT with a heavy stress on the middle syllable.

conversation.text: She's really passionate about animal rescue.
What are you passionate about outside of work?
He gets so passionate about coffee; don't get him started.

core.definition: A king of the northern kingdom of Israel (about 737 to 732 BCE) who came to power by assassination and allied with Aram against Judah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final vowel is a reduced uh, not a long ay or a hard k sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical name used in biblical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Pekah is a name you will hear in Bible study, sermons and church history discussions. Americans say it as a proper name without any special register. Note that he is different from Pekahiah, his predecessor.

examples.everyday: Have you read about King Pekah in Second Kings? He sounds like a real schemer.
examples.professional: In my sermon on Isaiah 7, I will explain why Pekah and Rezin threatened Jerusalem.
examples.analytical: The Syro-Ephraimite alliance under Pekah and Rezin provides the historical setting for Isaiah's warning to Ahaz.

nuance.analogy: Pekah is like a usurper who seizes a throne with a knife and then makes a dangerous alliance to protect it.
common_mistakes: Confusing Pekah with Pekahiah, the king he overthrew.
Pronouncing the name with a long a at the end.
nuance.biblical_note: Pekah son of Remaliah was a king of Israel who, according to 2 Kings 15:25, killed Pekahiah and took the throne. In 2 Kings 15:29 he is shown losing much of northern Israel to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria. In Isaiah 7:1 he joins Rezin of Aram in an attack on Judah under Ahaz, which prompts Isaiah's message of reassurance. Scripture presents him as a king who led Israel into political disaster by opposing God's plan for the house of David.

senses.definition: Allowing the passage of light; translucent or transparent.
Easily understood; clear.
Of music or some other sound: not discordant or harsh; clear and pure-sounding.
Of a person, their mind, etc.: able to think and understand clearly; not confused; clear, sharp.

core.definition: Very clear, so that light passes through easily; also used for writing or speech that is easy to understand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced uh, and the last syllable is a short id, not a long eye.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises clarity, whether in water, glass or prose.
nuance.usage_note: Pellucid is a formal and literary word, used mostly in writing and in polished speech. Americans would usually say 'clear' or 'transparent' in everyday talk. It is a good choice in an essay, a review or a formal speech, but it may sound stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Transparent is common and neutral, while pellucid is more literary and suggests especially bright, pure clarity.
Translucent means letting light through but not clearly showing objects, while pellucid implies you can see right through.

examples.everyday: The lake was so pellucid in the morning that we could see the fish near the bottom.
examples.professional: Your summary of the project was pellucid, so the executives understood the risk right away.
examples.analytical: The author's pellucid style makes the most difficult argument in the book easy to follow.

nuance.analogy: A pellucid explanation is like a clean window: you look through it and see the subject as it really is.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pellucidus, from per- 'through' and lucidus 'clear, bright'.
common_mistakes: Using pellucid for ordinary transparent objects in casual speech, where clear would sound more natural.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PEL-yoo-sid'.

pellucid.etymology: The adjective is a Latin *pellūcidus*, *perlucidus* (“transparent, pellucid; very bright; very understandable”), from *per-* + *lūcidus* (“clear; full of light, bright, shining; easily understood, clear, lucid”) (from *lūceō* (“to shine; to become visible,…

senses.definition: In a peremptory manner; in a commanding tone, brooking no delay.
senses.example: He was peremptorily summoned to see the commanding officer.

core.definition: In a bossy, commanding way that allows no argument or delay.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REMP, the second syllable. The first and middle syllables are very reduced, and the 'ily' ending sounds like 'uh-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an abrupt, bossy manner that gives no room for discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in formal writing or describing a boss, official or customer who gives orders without discussion. It sounds stiff in casual talk, where 'bossily' or 'in a bossy way' is more natural. Use it to describe how someone said something, not to describe a whole situation.

distinctions.note: Abruptly describes something sudden, while peremptorily stresses a commanding tone that brooks no objection.
Curtly means shortly and rudely, while peremptorily specifically means ordering without allowing delay or debate.

examples.everyday: When I asked if I could pay later, the cashier said peremptorily that it had to be paid now.
examples.professional: The manager peremptorily cut off the discussion and assigned the tasks without taking questions.
examples.analytical: The judge rejected the motion peremptorily, refusing to hear any argument on the procedural question.

nuance.analogy: Speaking peremptorily is like a traffic officer who points at the road and waves you on without stopping to explain.
nuance.etymology: From Latin peremptorius, 'deadly, decisive', from perimere, 'to destroy, to cut off'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'peremptory' and 'preemptive', which are different words.
Stressing the first syllable instead of REMP.

senses.definition: A materialistic attitude accompanied by ignorance of artistic or cultural matters.

core.definition: An attitude of materialism combined with ignorance of or hostility toward art, culture, and learning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIS, the second syllable. The final syllable -ism is a weak 'um,' and the middle -in- is a short 'ih.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a critical attitude, often used to condemn materialism and indifference to culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use philistinism in literary criticism, cultural commentary, and essays about education or public life. It is an abstract noun for a general attitude, not for a single person. In casual talk, people more often say someone is a philistine or does not care about the arts.

distinctions.note: Materialism is a general focus on possessions and money, whereas philistinism is materialism combined with contempt for or ignorance of culture.
Anti-intellectualism is hostility to ideas and thinking in general, while philistinism is specifically about art and culture.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the philistinism in some of these reality shows drives me crazy.
examples.professional: Management's philistinism about the design budget made it hard to justify any investment in good typography.
examples.analytical: Arnold's critique of English middle-class philistinism argued that material success had blinded society to the value of culture and ideas.

nuance.analogy: Philistinism is like a house with fine windows that no one ever opens, because no one can see the view.
nuance.etymology: From philistine, with the suffix -ism, the 19th-century English usage based on the German Philister.
common_mistakes: Using philistinism to name a single person; the word names an attitude, so say a philistine for a person.
Confusing it with philistine, the adjective or person, when you need the abstract noun.

senses.definition: To do by guessing, intuition, or trial and error; to react to events as they occur, often with risk of negative outcomes; to improvise.
senses.example: If they ask for something we didn't prepare, we will have to play it by ear.

senses.definition: To play guided by one's musical perception and intuition, rather than from a written score.

core.definition: To decide what to do as events happen, rather than following a fixed plan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ear, and the phrase links smoothly: 'play-i-ty-BY-EER.' The r in ear is pronounced in American speech, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound relaxed and flexible, or careless if the situation needs planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use play it by ear for travel, parties, dinners and work when plans are uncertain. A natural reply is 'Sounds good, we'll see how it goes.' In serious business or safety matters, saying it can sound like you are not prepared, so use it with friends and family more than with bosses.

distinctions.note: Wing it means improvising with little or no preparation, often with a sense of risk; play it by ear suggests waiting to see what happens before deciding.
Go with the flow is more passive, while play it by ear implies making active decisions as you go.

collocations: play it by ear for now
decide to play it by ear

examples.everyday: We don't know if the kids will be tired, so let's play it by ear tonight.
examples.professional: Until the vendor confirms the date, we'll play it by ear and adjust the schedule as needed.
examples.analytical: The method cannot be fully specified in advance, so the researchers play it by ear at each stage.

nuance.analogy: Like a jazz musician who listens and responds to the band, you adjust to what happens instead of reading from a score.
nuance.etymology: From the musical sense of playing a tune by ear, without reading music, which was extended to general improvisation.
common_mistakes: Using it for a detailed plan; it means flexible decision making, not preparation.
Dropping the it: say 'play it by ear,' not 'play by ear' in casual speech.

synonyms: make it up as one goes along
fly by the seat of one's pants

conversation.text: We don't have plans for Saturday. Let's play it by ear.
I'm not sure how long the meeting will go, so let's play it by ear.
"When should I come over?" "Let's play it by ear depending on traffic."

senses.definition: The production or the condition of polarity.
The grouping of opinions into two extremes.
The production of polarized light; the direction in which the electric field of an electromagnetic wave points.
The separation of positive and negative charges in a nucleus, atom, molecule or system.
