examples.analytical: The book of Esther sets its story in the citadel of Susa, which gives the narrative a courtly and political setting.

nuance.analogy: Susa is like Washington, D.C., for the Persian empire: a seat of government where royal decisions were made.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Sousa, from Elamite Šušan, the name of the city.
common_mistakes: Confusing Susa with Susanna, who is a person in the book of Daniel.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Susa appears in the Bible as Shushan, the Hebrew name for the city. The Hebrew word Shushan is probably of Elamite origin, though the Hebrew word shoshan means lily. Esther 1:2 places the Persian king's palace at Shushan the castle, Nehemiah 1:1 names Shushan the castle as where Nehemiah was, and Daniel 8:2 has Daniel in a vision at Shushan in the province of Elam.

senses.definition: Interacting with other elements in series; blocking; interacting with the same program or thread as other operations, thereby preventing those operations from resuming until the operation of interest is complete.
At the same time, at the same frequency.

core.definition: Happening at the same time or at the same rate; in computing, an operation that waits for another to finish before continuing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a weak 'us' sound, not 'ous'. The 'ch' sound is a hard 'k', so say SING-kruh-nus, not SING-chruh-nus.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes timing and is precise rather than emotional.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech Americans usually say 'at the same time' rather than synchronous. The word is common in software, engineering, and education, where synchronous classes (live, real-time) are contrasted with asynchronous ones. Using it in casual conversation may sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: Simultaneous means happening at the same moment; synchronous can also imply a regular, ongoing coordination of rhythm or flow.
Asynchronous means not occurring at the same time; synchronous is its opposite and is the standard contrast in online learning and messaging.

examples.everyday: Our class is synchronous, so we all log in at 7 p.m. to talk live.
examples.professional: We need synchronous calls for the design review, but the status updates can stay asynchronous.
examples.analytical: A synchronous process blocks until the result is available, which makes its control flow easier to reason about.

nuance.analogy: Like an orchestra playing from the same sheet music at the same tempo.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synchronos, from syn- (together) and chronos (time).
common_mistakes: Confusing synchronous with simultaneous in casual contexts where simultaneous is more natural.
Mispronouncing the stress or adding a syllable, as in sin-CROW-nus.

synchronous.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *synchronus*, from Ancient Greek *σύγχρονος* (“contemporaneous”), from *σῠν-* (“with, together”) + *χρόνος* (“time”).

senses.definition: To combine two or more things to produce a new product.
senses.example: synthesize data

senses.definition: To be combined producing a new, more complex product.
To produce a substance by chemical synthesis.
senses.example: The lab was able to synthesize a new compound.

senses.definition: To be produced by chemical synthesis.

core.definition: To combine separate elements, ideas or data into a single coherent whole, or to produce something new by combining parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is reduced. The final syllable rhymes with eyes, not with cheese, so the word has three clear beats.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests skill and creativity in bringing things together intelligently.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synthesize in business, science and writing, as in 'we need to synthesize the feedback.' In casual speech they usually say put together or pull together. Chemists also use it for making compounds, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Combine is general and neutral; synthesize implies the parts are merged into something new and coherent.
Summarize shortens material; synthesize integrates several sources or ideas into a new whole.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to synthesize everything my friends told me about the job offer.
examples.professional: Can you synthesize the feedback from the last three sprints into one slide?
examples.analytical: A good theology paper does not merely list positions; it synthesizes them into a coherent argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a chef who blends separate ingredients into a single sauce, synthesize means bringing many parts into one coherent dish.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from synthesis, which comes from Greek syntithenai, 'to put together'.
common_mistakes: Using synthesize as a noun; the noun is synthesis
Using it for simple copying or collecting, when the meaning requires real integration

senses.definition: A series of small, intricate dishes made using special techniques or with unusual or seasonal ingredients, served as a restaurant dining experience.

core.definition: A multicourse meal at a restaurant made of several small dishes, often chosen by the chef and showing special techniques or seasonal ingredients.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is strongest on menu, and taste keeps a secondary stress. In fast speech, 'tasting menu' sounds like 'TAY-sting MEH-nyoo,' with the t flapped in some speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a special, carefully designed dining experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tasting menu at upscale or chef-driven restaurants, usually for a higher price than a regular dinner. You might ask, 'Do you have a tasting menu?' or 'Should we do the tasting menu?' A natural reply is 'Yes, it's about seven courses, and the chef chooses everything.'

distinctions.note: A prix fixe menu is a set-price menu with a limited number of choices, while a tasting menu is usually a chef's selection of several small courses.
A la carte means each dish is ordered and priced separately, while a tasting menu is a single planned sequence of courses.

collocations: wine pairing with a tasting menu

examples.everyday: We should try the tasting menu for your birthday because the chef makes everything fresh.
examples.professional: The client dinner will be a tasting menu, so the sommelier should plan pairings with the courses.
examples.analytical: The tasting menu reframes dining as a narrative, where each small course advances a larger argument about place and season.

nuance.analogy: A tasting menu is like a short album where each track shows a different side of the artist.
nuance.etymology: From taste, a verb meaning to sample flavor, plus menu, from the French menu.
common_mistakes: Saying a tasting menu means a menu for tasting wine only.
Using a plural article incorrectly, such as 'a tasting menus' instead of 'a tasting menu' or 'tasting menus' in general.

conversation.text: For our anniversary, we did the seven-course tasting menu.
The tasting menu takes about three hours, so don't plan anything after.
Is the tasting menu available for vegetarians?

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a tempest; also, of a place: frequently experiencing tempests; (very) stormy.

Characterized by disorderly, frenetic, or violent activity; stormy, tumultuous, turbulent; also, of a person, their behavior or nature, etc.: characterized by bouts of bad temper or sudden changes of mood; impetuous, stormy, temperamental.
senses.example: After their tempestuous argument, they did not speak to each other for weeks.

core.definition: Very stormy or turbulent, or describing emotional behavior that is wild, unpredictable, and full of conflict.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -PES, and the -tu- sounds like 'choo' in American speech. The final -ous is a reduced 'us', not 'oos'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dramatic. It suggests violence, turmoil, or intense emotion, and it can be used with admiration in literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tempestuous mostly in writing, reviews, and literary discussion, especially for storms, relationships, or periods of conflict. It is less common in casual speech, where stormy or intense is more natural. You might hear a tempestuous relationship in a movie review or a tempestuous meeting in a news story.

distinctions.note: Stormy is the everyday word for weather or a rough situation, while tempestuous is more formal and suggests emotional or dramatic turmoil.
Turbulent is common in business and science for unstable conditions, while tempestuous adds a more emotional or literary tone.
Temperamental describes unpredictable moods or machines, while tempestuous suggests greater violence or drama.

examples.everyday: They had a tempestuous marriage full of loud fights and sudden reconciliations.
examples.professional: The quarter was tempestuous, with three reorganizations and two sudden budget freezes.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's prose mirrors the tempestuous inner lives of his characters, whose passions break every social rule.

nuance.analogy: A tempestuous relationship is like a sailboat in a sudden storm: it moves fast, tips often, and never stays calm for long.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tempestas, meaning storm, with the suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as tem-PES-too-us with a full 'oo' sound in the middle.
Using tempestuous as a noun; it is an adjective, so say a tempestuous period, not a tempestuous.

tempestuous.etymology: From Late Middle English *tempestious*, *tempestous*, *tempestuous* (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous”), from Anglo-Norman *tempestous*, and Old French *tempesteus*, *tempestos*, *tempestous*, *tempestuose*, and directly from its etymon Latin *tempestuōsus*…

senses.definition: That can be safely accessed from multiple threads.

core.definition: Describing code or data that can be used by several threads at the same time without causing errors or corrupted results.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'safe', and 'thread' is lighter. Say 'thred-SAFE' as two clear word units with a short vowel in 'thread'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in technical reviews. It signals reliable, well-designed code.
nuance.usage_note: Developers in the United States say 'thread-safe' in code reviews, design documents, and standups. It is a technical term and rarely used outside software engineering. If a library is not safe, engineers say it is 'not thread-safe' rather than 'unsafe'.

distinctions.note: 'Concurrent' means that several things happen at overlapping times. 'Thread-safe' means that concurrent access will not break the data or behavior.
A reentrant function can be interrupted and called again before finishing. A thread-safe function can be called from several threads at once, which is a related but different property.

examples.everyday: My roommate fixed the bug, but she says the cache is still not thread-safe.
examples.professional: Before we merge this, let's make sure the cache is thread-safe under heavy load.
examples.analytical: A method is thread-safe when its correctness does not depend on the order in which concurrent threads interleave their operations.

nuance.analogy: A thread-safe structure is like a shared whiteboard with one marker rule, so two people can write without erasing each other's work.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'thread' and 'safe', from the late twentieth-century computing vocabulary.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'thread safe', in technical documents; the hyphen is standard.
Pronouncing 'thread' with a long vowel, as in 'thread' the verb.

senses.definition: Introducing a short version of, or simply the conclusion of, a relevant story.
senses.example: Anyway, long story short, I totally screwed up today.

core.definition: Used to introduce the brief ending or main point of a longer story, skipping the details.

pronunciation.respelling: too mayk uh lawng STOR-ee SHORT
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SHORT, while 'story' keeps a secondary stress. 'Story' is pronounced with a clear American r, and 'a' reduces to 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals courtesy toward the listener's time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this at the start of a conclusion when the story has been long or tangled. It is conversational and often said with a laugh. A natural reply is 'Okay, what happened in the end?' Avoid it in formal writing, where 'in summary' is better.

distinctions.note: 'In short' summarizes the main point at any length, while this phrase specifically promises to skip the details of a long story.
'Bottom line' emphasizes the key result; this phrase emphasizes shortening a story.

collocations: to make a long story short
let me make a long story short
to make a long story short, we moved
I'll make a long story short

examples.everyday: To make a long story short, my flight got canceled and I slept at the airport.
examples.professional: To make a long story short, the vendor missed the deadline, so we are moving the launch to next quarter.
examples.analytical: To make a long story short, the argument collapses once we separate the premise from the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like skipping to the last chapter of a novel when your friend is rambling about the plot.
nuance.etymology: English idiom from the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a short story long' by accident; the phrase has the long story made short.
Dropping 'a' or 'to', as in 'make long story short'.

to-make-a-long-story-short.etymology: A reduced form of *to cut a long story short* and *to make a long story short*.

conversation.text: To make a long story short, the car broke down and we had to walk.
They argued for an hour, but to make a long story short, they're getting married.
To make a long story short, I'm moving back to Texas.

senses.definition: Very hot and dry.
Full of intense emotions arising from sexual love; ardent and passionate.
senses.example: a torrid love scene in a film or novel

senses.definition: Full of difficulty.
[of a streak, form, etc.] Good; impressive; hot.

core.definition: Very hot and dry; also full of passionate, intense emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a short i, so say TOR-id, not TOR-eed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for heat, positive or romantic for passion, and negative for difficult situations.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, torrid is most common for very hot weather, such as a torrid summer or torrid days in Texas. It can also describe a passionate romance, usually in writing or in movie descriptions. Casual speakers more often say scorching or blazing for heat.

distinctions.note: Hot is everyday and neutral. Torrid is more intense and often suggests dryness and extreme heat.
Scorching is casual and vivid for heat. Torrid is more literary and can also describe passion.

examples.everyday: It's been torrid all week, so let's get the pool open early.
examples.professional: We had a torrid pace last quarter, so the team needs a breather before the next launch.
examples.analytical: The poet's torrid language pushes against the restraint of his age, showing desire as a force that overwhelms reason.

nuance.analogy: Like a desert at noon: dry, bright, and too hot to stay outside for long.
nuance.etymology: From Latin torridus, 'dried up or parched,' from torrere, 'to parch.'
common_mistakes: Using torrid for mild warmth; it means very hot and intense.
Confusing torrid with torrent; they share a root but mean different things.

senses.definition: To give off (vapor, waste matter etc.); to exhale (an odor etc.).
To become known; to escape from secrecy.
senses.example: It eventually transpired that the murder victim had been a notorious blackmailer.

senses.definition: To happen, take place.
Of plants, to give off water and waste products through the stomata.

core.definition: To happen or take place, especially something that is discovered or revealed later; also, to become known.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPY, the second syllable, and the final -er is a reduced r sound. Avoid pronouncing the middle s as a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It often appears in news or formal speech about events that come out over time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transpire in news and formal speech, usually about events that become known later, as in it transpired that. In casual talk, people more often say happen or turn out. Avoid using transpire to mean happen in a simple, everyday event; it sounds stiff.

distinctions.note: Happen is the everyday word; transpire often suggests a discovery of what happened, and it sounds more formal.
Occur is neutral and common; transpire is more formal and often used with a revealed fact.

examples.everyday: It turned out that the restaurant had closed early, and nobody told us what transpired.
examples.professional: Please send me a summary of what transpired during the vendor call so the team can follow up.
examples.analytical: It transpired that the committee had withheld key evidence, which changed the outcome of the entire inquiry.

nuance.analogy: Transpire is like a secret slowly coming out of a sealed room: the event was there all along, but only later becomes known.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin transpirare, to breathe through, from trans- (through) and spirare (to breathe).
common_mistakes: Using transpire as a simple synonym for happen in everyday speech; it sounds formal and can sound odd.
Confusing transpire with perspire, which means to sweat.

transpire.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *transpirer*, from Medieval Latin *transpirare* (“to breathe through”), from Latin *trans* (“across”) *spirare* (“to breathe”).

senses.definition: Having no boundaries or limits.
senses.example: The universe is finite but unbounded.

core.definition: Having no boundaries, limits, or end, so that something can grow or continue without restriction.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BOWN, the second syllable. The final -ed is pronounced as a short id sound, not as a separate syllable like ed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can describe infinite possibility or a lack of constraint, and in technical settings it is simply a precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unbounded in mathematics, science, and formal writing, and sometimes in describing ambition or enthusiasm. In everyday speech people more often say 'endless' or 'no limit.' In mathematics, unbounded has a specific meaning, so use it precisely when discussing functions or sequences.

distinctions.note: Boundless is more emotional or poetic and often describes love or energy, while unbounded is more technical and precise.
Infinite is a stronger mathematical word for something without end, while unbounded means without an upper or lower limit, which may or may not be infinite.

examples.everyday: My little brother has unbounded energy, so I can't keep up with him at the park.
examples.professional: If the model's loss function is unbounded below, the optimization can diverge, so we need a regularization term.
examples.analytical: Hegel's idea of the infinite is not an unbounded series of finite things, but a totality that contains its own limits.

nuance.analogy: An unbounded space is like an open field with no fences, where you can keep walking without reaching an edge.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus bounded, from bound, from Old French bonde, meaning limit or boundary.
common_mistakes: Confusing unbounded with infinite: a function can be unbounded without going to infinity in every direction.
Using unbounded to mean unlimited money or resources in casual speech, which can sound overly technical.

senses.definition: Not certain; unsure.
Not known for certain; questionable.
senses.example: Tomorrow's weather is uncertain.

senses.definition: Not yet determined; undecided.
Variable and subject to change.
Fitful or unsteady.
Unpredictable or capricious.
Something uncertain; everything uncertain.
senses.example: Their approach to the uncertain is laudable: they at least want to know the upper and lower bounds for what the answer could turn out to be.

core.definition: Not sure about something, or not known or decided yet; unclear or doubtful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUR, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'tun', not 'tain'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an honest lack of knowledge, but it can sound anxious when used about one's own feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uncertain in everyday speech for not being sure, as in 'I'm uncertain about the time.' It is also common in business and news contexts for situations that are not yet settled. Unsure is more casual and personal, while uncertain sounds slightly more formal.

distinctions.note: Unsure is casual and usually describes a person's own feelings, while uncertain can describe situations, outcomes, or facts.
Doubtful suggests you believe something is unlikely, while uncertain means the outcome or fact is not known either way.

examples.everyday: I'm still uncertain whether we're going to the lake this weekend.
examples.professional: The launch date is uncertain until the vendor confirms the integration tests.
examples.analytical: Paul's warning about the uncertain value of wealth challenges the assumption that possessions offer security.

nuance.analogy: Like a fog over a road: you can see the next few steps, but not clearly where the road leads.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English, from 'un-' (not) and 'certain', from Old French 'certain', from Latin 'certus' meaning settled or sure.
common_mistakes: Using uncertain to describe a person who is unsure, when unsure is the more natural word in everyday speech.
Stressing the wrong syllable, or pronouncing the final syllable as 'tain'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is adēlotēs (ἀδηλότης), meaning uncertainty or unpredictability. In 1 Timothy 6:17 Paul warns the rich not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches but on God, who richly provides everything for our enjoyment. Paul's point is that wealth is unreliable compared with God's faithfulness.

senses.definition: Not suspecting; without any suspicion.
senses.example: He easily shot the unsuspecting target.

core.definition: Not aware of a danger, trick or deception; trusting and unaware of what is about to happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPEK, and the first syllables are reduced. Do not stress SUS as in the noun 'SUS-pect', because the adjective stresses the verb-like second part.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative for the person, since they are vulnerable to being tricked or harmed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unsuspecting in news, crime stories and everyday talk about people being scammed or surprised: 'unsuspecting tourists' or 'unsuspecting customers.' Casual speakers often prefer 'didn't see it coming.' The word is slightly formal but never rude.

distinctions.note: Naive describes someone with little experience of the world; unsuspecting describes being unaware of one specific threat right now.
Unaware is neutral and general; unsuspecting emphasizes vulnerability to a trick or attack.

examples.everyday: The scam calls target unsuspecting older people who think they are speaking to their bank.
examples.professional: The phishing email targeted unsuspecting employees who believed it came from the HR department.
examples.analytical: Good suspense stories rely on unsuspecting readers, whose trust lets the author surprise them with a sudden turn.

nuance.analogy: A swimmer who doesn't notice the current until it has already carried them far from shore.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus suspecting, from Latin suspicere, to look up at, to mistrust.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable like the noun 'SUS-pect'
Using it to mean simply uninformed; it implies a possible threat or trick

senses.definition: Difficult to carry, handle, manage or operate because of its size, weight, shape or complexity.
Badly managed or operated.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: Hard to carry, handle, or control because of its size, weight, shape, or complexity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, WEEL, and the first syllable is reduced to a quick 'un'. Don't pronounce the 'w' as a 'v' or stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that is awkward or inconvenient to manage, often in a way that slows things down.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for physical objects like a large couch, a bundle of lumber, or a huge cardboard box, and also for systems or processes that are too complicated, such as 'an unwieldy bureaucracy.' Saying it about a person sounds rude, so describe their situation instead. In casual talk, 'awkward' or 'clumsy' are common alternatives.

distinctions.note: Clumsy describes a person's movements or a poorly made action; unwieldy describes an object or system that is hard to handle because of its size or complexity.
Cumbersome is very close in meaning and often describes slow, heavy procedures; unwieldy more often describes something physically hard to hold or steer.

examples.everyday: Moving that old sofa up the stairs was a nightmare because it was so unwieldy.
examples.professional: Our release process has become unwieldy, so we need to split it into smaller deployments.
examples.analytical: A constitution that is too detailed can become unwieldy, since every amendment must navigate an ever-growing web of clauses.

nuance.analogy: Think of trying to steer a shopping cart with a broken wheel: it has the mass, but not the easy control you need.
nuance.etymology: From 'un-' (not) plus 'wieldy,' from the old verb 'wield' meaning to control or handle.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'un-WIL-dee' with a short i, when the vowel is a long ee sound, as in 'wield'.
Using it for a person, as in 'He is unwieldy,' which sounds insulting.

senses.definition: The act of validating something.
Something, such as a certificate, that validates something; attestation, authentication, confirmation, proof or verification.
The process whereby others confirm the validity of one's emotions or perspective.
The process of identifying a new prisoner's gang affiliation.

core.definition: The process of checking that something is correct, accurate, or acceptable, or the approval that results from such a check.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, DAY. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun', and the middle vowels are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. In emotional contexts it can be warm, meaning acceptance of someone's feelings.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, 'validation' often refers to testing or approval, as in 'validation testing'. In personal conversation it can mean emotional acceptance, as in 'I just needed some validation.' Americans may also use it for the process of checking a document or identity.

distinctions.note: 'Verification' usually means proving that something is true. 'Validation' often means checking that something meets a standard or works for its purpose.
'Approval' means permission or agreement from someone in authority. 'Validation' is a process of checking or confirming, often with evidence.

examples.everyday: After I told her about my divorce, she gave me the validation I needed just by listening.
examples.professional: We need validation on the new billing feature before the release goes out next Friday.
examples.analytical: Scholars look for independent validation of a historical claim before accepting it as established.

nuance.analogy: Validation is like a second pair of eyes checking a form before it is submitted.
nuance.etymology: From validate, from Latin validus 'strong, effective'.
common_mistakes: Using 'validation' for simple agreement; it usually implies a check or confirmation process.
Mispronouncing it as 'val-ih-DAY-shuhn' with a heavy final syllable; the ending should be a clear but quick 'shun'.

core.definition: Written to operate on whole arrays at once instead of looping over single values, which makes numerical code much faster.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VEK. The final '-ized' is one short syllable that sounds like 'rized', not 'ry-zed'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests faster, cleaner code.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and engineers in America often praise code by calling it 'vectorized', meaning it avoids slow Python loops. You will hear it in code reviews and in tutorials on NumPy or pandas. Outside technical settings the word is not used.

distinctions.note: A loop-based approach processes one value at a time; a vectorized approach handles the whole array in one operation.
Parallel code runs tasks at the same time on several processors; vectorized code uses array operations, often within one processor.

examples.everyday: My son's science project ran so fast after we made the code vectorized that we couldn't believe it.
examples.professional: The vectorized version of the function cut the runtime from an hour to under two minutes.
examples.analytical: A vectorized implementation expresses the algorithm in terms of whole-array operations, which makes its mathematical structure more visible.

nuance.analogy: Vectorized code is like a bakery that makes a whole tray of cookies at once instead of shaping each cookie by hand.
nuance.etymology: From 'vectorize', from 'vector', from Latin 'vector', carrier, with the past-participle ending '-ed'.
common_mistakes: Using 'vectorized' to mean 'faster' in general; the word refers specifically to array-based operations.
Stressing the final syllable, which makes the word sound like a different verb.

senses.definition: To say defamatory things about someone or something; to speak ill of.
To belittle through speech; to put down.

core.definition: To speak or write about someone in a very negative and damaging way, often unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are short and reduced, and the final -fy rhymes with 'sky.' Many learners pronounce the final syllable as 'fee.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies unfair or harsh attacks on someone's character or reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vilify mainly in news, politics, and serious discussion, such as 'the media vilified the senator.' It is more formal than 'trash-talk' or 'bash,' which are casual. In everyday speech, 'badmouth' or 'attack' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Criticize can be fair and constructive; vilify implies unfair, harsh, and damaging attacks.
Defame usually has a legal sense of spreading false statements; vilify focuses on harsh, hostile language.

examples.everyday: My brother got vilified online just because he disagreed with a popular TV show.
examples.professional: Our manager should not let the team vilify a colleague who made an honest mistake in the report.
examples.analytical: Historians caution against vilifying political rivals, since such caricatures obscure the actual choices they made.

nuance.analogy: To vilify someone is like painting a dark, ugly picture of them and then hanging it where everyone can see.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin vilificare, 'to disparage,' from Latin vilis, 'cheap,' and facere, 'to make.'
common_mistakes: Using vilify for mild disagreement; it implies strong, unfair hostility.
Stressing the second syllable (vi-LIF-ih-fy).

senses.definition: Asking how much you pay at the visit under your insurance.

core.definition: A question asking how much you must pay at a medical visit under your health insurance plan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of 'copay', which is pronounced like 'KOH-pay'. Americans say 'copay' as one smooth word, not 'co-pay' with two equal stresses.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. Asking about it shows you are managing your costs, which is normal and expected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this when booking an appointment, calling a clinic, or at the front desk before a visit, since copays are set by insurance. The answer is usually a fixed dollar amount, such as 'Thirty dollars for a specialist visit.' It is common and polite; the full term 'copayment' is used on forms and in formal insurance language.

distinctions.note: A copay is a fixed amount for a service, while a deductible is the total you must pay yourself each year before insurance begins paying most costs.
Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost you share with insurance, while a copay is a flat fee per visit.

examples.everyday: I'm booking a visit for my back. What's the copay for a regular doctor?
examples.professional: Before we schedule the imaging, can you tell me what the copay is so I can quote the patient accurately?
examples.analytical: The question 'What's the copay?' exposes how insurance design shifts financial risk onto patients while appearing to offer predictable care costs.

nuance.analogy: It is like a cover charge at the door: a set amount you pay each time you walk in.
common_mistakes: Saying 'co-pay' with two stressed syllables; in American speech it is one word, 'copay'.
Confusing copay with deductible; a copay is due at the visit, while a deductible is a yearly total.

conversation.text: What's the copay for a regular visit?
What's the copay for this? Do I pay now or later?
What's the copay if I go to urgent care instead?

senses.definition: A windstorm of limited extent, such as a tornado, dust devil, or waterspout, characterized by an inward spiral motion of the air with an upward current in the center; a vortex of air.
A person or body of objects or events sweeping violently onward.
senses.example: Once he got that new scooter he turned into a whirlwind and damaged all the flowers.

senses.definition: Rapid and minimal.
senses.example: a whirlwind tour, a whirlwind romance

core.definition: A rapidly spinning column of air, or a period of very fast, busy, and often chaotic activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'WURL,' and make the second syllable a short 'wind' rhyming with 'pinned,' not 'wined' or 'find.' The 'h' is optional and usually silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing excitement, such as 'a whirlwind romance,' and negative when describing chaos or disaster.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'whirlwind' for a fast, exciting period, such as 'a whirlwind tour' or 'a whirlwind weekend.' As a physical storm, it may refer to a small dust devil or a tornado. Use it for something that moved quickly and left you breathless.

distinctions.note: A tornado is a violent, funnel-shaped storm cloud, while 'whirlwind' is a general term for a spinning column of air.
A dust devil is a small, harmless whirlwind in dry areas, while 'whirlwind' can describe any size or strength.

examples.everyday: We had a whirlwind weekend in Chicago, so I'm still exhausted from all the walking.
examples.professional: The product launch was a whirlwind of last-minute changes and late-night calls.
examples.analytical: The reform passed in a whirlwind of legislative activity, leaving little room for public debate.

nuance.analogy: A whirlwind is like a spinning top of air that picks up everything in its path and carries it along.
nuance.etymology: From 'whirl' and 'wind,' combining the idea of spinning with moving air.
common_mistakes: Using 'whirlwind' only for physical storms and missing the figurative sense for busy periods.
Pronouncing the 'w' as a 'v' or mixing up 'whirlwind' with 'windmill.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word se'arah (סְעָרָה) means a storm or whirlwind, and the RSV uses 'whirlwind' for a powerful manifestation of God. In Job 38:1 God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind, emphasizing divine sovereignty over creation. In 2 Kings 2:1 Elijah goes up to heaven by a whirlwind, and in Isaiah 66:15 the LORD's chariots are described as like the whirlwind in judgment.

senses.definition: (To cause) to become white or whiter; to bleach or blanch.
senses.example: Age had whitened his hair.

senses.definition: To increase the security of an iterated block cipher by steps that combine the data with portions of the key.
To normalize data so that the covariance matrix becomes the identity matrix; i.e. to remove correlations so each variable has unit variance.

core.definition: To make something white or whiter, or to become white, as with teeth, walls, or laundry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending -en is a syllabic n with no separate vowel, so say it as a single light syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts. In skin-color contexts it can be sensitive, so avoid it when talking about people's skin.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually use 'whiten' for teeth, grout, walls, and fabric, and often say 'whitening' for products such as toothpaste. The word is common in data science and statistics for a specific transformation, which is a technical use. For cleaning with chemicals, many Americans prefer 'bleach'.

distinctions.note: To bleach uses chemicals to remove color, while whiten means simply to make something look whiter.
Whitewash can mean to paint with a lime mixture or to hide wrongdoing, so it has a negative sense that whiten lacks.
Brighten means to make something lighter or more vivid in general, while whiten specifically means to make it white.

examples.everyday: This toothpaste says it can whiten your teeth in about two weeks.
examples.professional: Before we publish the chart, we whiten the background so the labels stand out clearly.
examples.analytical: Rabbinic and early Christian readers treated whiteness in Scripture as a sign of purity, so to whiten a garment was also to describe moral cleansing.

nuance.analogy: Whitening is like sunlight slowly bleaching a faded shirt until it looks new again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hwitian, from hwit meaning white.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two full syllables, 'whi-ten', instead of one light final syllable.
Using 'whiten' for skin in ordinary conversation, where it can sound offensive.
Confusing whiten with whitewash when the meaning is to cover up or paint.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the verb lābhan means to make white. Isaiah 1:18 (RSV) says that sins as red as crimson shall become white as snow, which uses whiteness as an image of forgiveness. Psalm 51:7 asks God to wash the psalmist so that he is whiter than snow, expressing the desire for inner cleansing. Daniel 12:10 speaks of many who will purify and make themselves white in a time of testing.

whiten.etymology: From Middle English *whitenen*, *whitnen*, from Old Norse *hvítna* (“to whiten”), from Proto-Germanic **hwītnōną* (“to whiten, become white”), from Proto-Indo-European **kwind-*, **kwint-* (“bright”), equivalent to *white* + *en*.

senses.definition: Any of various deciduous trees or shrubs in the genus Salix, in the willow family Salicaceae, found primarily on moist soils in cooler zones in the northern hemisphere.
The wood of these trees.
A rotating spiked drum used to open and clean cotton heads.
A cricket bat.
The baseball bat.
To open and cleanse (cotton, flax, wool, etc.) by means of a willow.
To form a shape or move in a way similar to the long, slender branches of a willow.

core.definition: A tree or shrub with long, thin, flexible branches that grows near rivers, lakes, and wet ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable ends in an oh sound, so say WIL-oh, not WIL-ow as in 'how'. The double l stays short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often evokes calm, gentle, grief, or quiet natural beauty in poetry and descriptions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use willow in everyday talk for the trees in parks or along creeks, such as weeping willow. In poetry, a willow often suggests sadness or flexibility. The word is common in gardening, landscaping and nature writing. A weeping willow is the most familiar American type.

distinctions.note: Poplars have broader leaves and stiffer, more upright branches; willows have narrow leaves and drooping, flexible branches.
Birch has white, papery bark; willow has rougher bark and grows in wetter soil.
Weeping willow is a specific type with very drooping branches; willow alone can refer to many species.

examples.everyday: Let's have our picnic under the big willow by the lake.
examples.professional: The landscape architect recommended planting native willow along the retention pond to stabilize the bank.
examples.analytical: The psalmist hangs his harp on the willows in Babylon, using the tree as an image of silent mourning in exile.

nuance.analogy: Like a ribbon of water-loving green: its long branches trail down like a flowing stream.
nuance.etymology: From Old English welig, willow tree.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'how' instead of 'oh'.
Using 'willow' for any tree: the word refers to Salix species, not to all trees that drape or droop.
nuance.biblical_note: Willows (Hebrew arabah, a word tied to the Arabah region and to willows by water) appear in Scripture as trees of moist places. Leviticus 23:40 lists willows of the brook among the branches used in the Feast of Booths. Psalm 137:2 describes the exiles hanging their harps on willows in Babylon as a sign of mourning. Isaiah 44:4 uses willows by flowing water as an image of growth and blessing that God gives to his people.

senses.definition: To take part in (a wrestling bout or match).
Sometimes followed by down: to contend with or move (someone) into or out of a position by grappling; also, to overcome (someone) by grappling.
To move or manipulate (something) using physical effort, usually with some difficulty or opposition.
senses.example: I couldn't wrestle the trunk down the hall.

senses.definition: To engage in (a contest or struggle).
To throw down (a calf or other livestock animal) for branding.
To grapple or otherwise contend with an opponent in order to throw or force them to the ground, chiefly as a sport or in unarmed combat.
Followed by with: to move or manipulate something using physical effort, usually with some difficulty or opposition.
To make one's way or move with some difficulty or effort.
Followed by against or with: to contend, to struggle; to exert effort, to strive.
A fight or struggle between people during which they grapple or otherwise contend with each other in order to throw or force their opponent to the ground, chiefly as a sport or in unarmed combat.
A situation in which people compete with each other; a contest, a struggle.
The action of contending or struggling.

core.definition: To struggle physically with someone, grappling to throw or pin them down; also, to struggle hard with a difficult problem or idea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The w is silent in the spelling but the r is pronounced, and the final -tle is a reduced syllable, so say 'RES-uhl' without a distinct t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be physical or figurative, and the figurative sense suggests serious effort rather than conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wrestle for sports and for figurative struggle, as in 'I wrestled with that decision all night.' The phrase 'wrestle with' is the common pattern for ideas, decisions, and doubts. Wrestle to the ground is a common expression for overpowering someone physically.

distinctions.note: Struggle is more general and can describe any difficulty, while wrestle often suggests physical grappling or close, sustained mental effort.
Grapple is close to wrestle in meaning and is often used figuratively, but grapple often implies holding on to a problem, while wrestle implies physical or intense effort.

collocations: wrestle the bag into the car

examples.everyday: I wrestled with whether to take the job all weekend.
examples.professional: We are still wrestling with the data migration, so the release may slip a few days.
examples.analytical: In Genesis 32:24 Jacob wrestles with a mysterious man until daybreak, and the struggle becomes a central image of faith in the narrative.

nuance.analogy: Wrestling with a problem is like untangling a knotted rope: you keep pulling, adjusting, and pulling again until the strands finally separate.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wrǣstlian, from wrǣstan, meaning to wrestle or struggle.
common_mistakes: Saying wrestle against a problem; the natural phrase is wrestle with.
Pronouncing the w, as in 'wres-tle'; the w is silent.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 32:24 the RSV says that Jacob was left alone and a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. Genesis 32:28 renames Jacob as one who has striven with God and with men. Ephesians 6:12 uses the Greek word palē for wrestling and says the struggle is not against flesh and blood. The Hebrew 'abaq in Genesis describes the struggle that defines Jacob's encounter.

wrestle.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *wrestlen,wrastlen* (“to engage in grappling combat or sport, struggle, wrestle; to twist and turn, squirm, wriggle, writhe; to contend, grapple with, struggle”), from Old English *wrǣstlian* (“to wrestle”), a form of…

senses.definition: To have a strong desire for something or to do something; to long for or to do something.
senses.example: All I yearn for is a simple life.

senses.definition: To long for something in the past with melancholy or nostalgia.
Of music, words, etc.: to express strong desire or longing.
Often followed by out: to perform (music) which conveys or say (words) which express strong desire or longing.
Of milk: to curdle, especially in the cheesemaking process.
Of cheese: to be made from curdled milk.
To curdle (milk), especially in the cheesemaking process.
To make (cheese) from curdled milk.
(dated) To have strong feelings of affection, love, sympathy, etc. toward someone.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A strong desire or longing; a yearning, a yen.

core.definition: To want something very much over a long period, especially something you cannot easily have; to long for it.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the American r-colored 'er' sound, like 'bird' with a 'y' in front. Do not add a separate r or an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use yearn in writing, speeches and emotional or literary contexts, such as yearning for home or freedom. In casual speech they more often say 'long for', 'miss' or 'really want'. The verb is often followed by 'for' or 'to'.

distinctions.note: Long for is more common in everyday speech and less intense; yearn sounds more emotional and sustained.
Crave suggests a strong physical or immediate appetite, such as for food; yearn suggests a deeper, longer longing.

examples.everyday: After three months on the road, I just yearn for my own bed and a quiet kitchen.
examples.professional: Our customers yearn for faster support, so the new help desk tool is a priority for this quarter.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker yearns for a lost home, and the verb carries both desire and grief, marking distance from what is longed for.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant leaning toward a window: the desire is steady and directed toward something out of reach.
nuance.etymology: From Old English giernan, meaning to desire or long for.
common_mistakes: Saying 'yearn to' when 'yearn for' is needed for a thing, as in 'yearn for peace' not 'yearn peace'
Pronouncing the vowel as 'yarn' or adding an extra syllable
nuance.biblical_note: Yearning in Scripture expresses deep longing for God, for home, or for others. Hebrew kamah (to long for, to pine after) appears in poetic passages about longing for God's presence, and the Greek epipotheō (ἐπιποθέω) describes intense longing, especially in Paul's letters. Psalm 84:2 expresses longing for the courts of the LORD, and 2 Corinthians 5:2 describes groaning and longing to be clothed with the heavenly dwelling. Philippians 1:8 says Paul yearns for the believers with the affection of Christ Jesus, showing that longing can be an expression of love for others.

yearn.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *yernen*, *yern* (“to express or feel desire; to desire, long or wish for; to lust after; to ask or demand for”), from Old English *ġeornan* (“to desire, yearn; to beg”), from **girnijan* (“to be eager for, desire”),…

core.definition: A place name in the Bible: one of the five cities of the Jordan plain, destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah, and also a valley in Benjamin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BOY. Keep the final syllable short and unstressed, and do not pronounce the middle vowel as a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet this name almost only in Bible study, sermons or reference works. It is not used in everyday talk. In a church setting you can say it simply as the name of an ancient town.

distinctions.note: Zebulun is a tribe and a son of Jacob, while Zeboiim is a city or valley, so the two names are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned Zeboiim in the sermon, and I had to look it up on my phone.
examples.professional: In the seminar handout, the lecturer listed Zeboiim alongside Sodom, Gomorrah and Admah as the cities of the plain.
examples.analytical: Genesis 10:19 and 14:2 name Zeboiim among the Canaanite cities, while Hosea 11:8 treats Admah and Zeboiim as examples of divine judgment.

nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew tseboyim, probably related to tsevi, 'gazelle', though the exact root is debated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in ZEB-oy-im.
Confusing Zeboiim with Zebulun or Zebul, which are different names.
nuance.biblical_note: Zeboiim (Hebrew tseboyim) names one of the cities of the Jordan plain. Genesis 10:19 lists it among the borders of Canaan, next to Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis 14:2 names its king, Shemeber, in the coalition that fought Chedorlaomer. Hosea 11:8 uses Admah and Zeboiim as a picture of the destruction God could have brought on Israel but did not.
